current_example.problem: Find the intersection of intervals $(-\infty, 3] \cap (0, \infty).$ Express the result as an inequality.
current_example.worked_solution:
We can start by sketching the two intervals $(-\infty, 3]$ and $(0, \infty)$ separately:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191341/assets/255da904e7d271006cef6a272379b8f160fc6cc9e5f8ede39d91141aea2eff7b.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191341/assets/31ad28b45aa2cefa4d83cc06710e9ae81446809ec0ac42da5baae36e235e35a9.png)

The intersection $(-\infty, 3] \cap (0, \infty)$ represents the values that are in both intervals. So, it can be graphed by finding where the two intervals overlap:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191341/assets/6a92713b9964c9b1583622553a7cdb3c9c700ecad95cc0581f1538d18d1fa42a.png)

Thus, $(-\infty, 3]\cap(0, \infty)={\color{blue}(0,3]}.$ This corresponds to the inequality

$$
0 < x \leq 3.
$$

**Watch out!** The point $0$ is not included in the intersection since it does not lie in the second interval. On the other hand, the point $3$ is included in the intersection because it lies in both intervals.
